subtitle: Work out what kind of leader you want to be and for whom: examine your own default picture of a good leader, turn your values into commitments that hold under pressure, and write and test a short purpose statement.
audience: For staff drawn to leading, with or without a title, and for new leads and supervisors who want to work out what kind of leader to be, whose interests their leadership serves and who it is for.

lessons.title: What a leadership purpose is and who it serves
objectives: Explain what a leadership purpose is and why it should name who it is for, drawing on the State's leader competency on self-awareness and growth.
Identify the groups your leadership serves, including people receiving services, colleagues and the public.
Describe whose experience is missing from your current picture of who your leadership is for.
Draft a first sentence of purpose that names who it is for and what should change for them.
lessons.teaching:
A leadership purpose is a short account of why you lead and for whom. Minnesota Management and Budget's Competency Definition Guide places self-awareness and growth first among the State's five leader competencies and defines it as a commitment to personal and professional growth through self-reflection and self-improvement. Its key skills include self-awareness, integrity, identity and cultural humility. The Guide also speaks of a State leader in any capacity, such as the head of a team, a committee or a partnership, so a purpose is worth writing whether or not you supervise anyone.

A first draft may describe the work without naming the people it serves. Phrases such as delivering quality results or supporting my team are true, but they could describe any job anywhere. They also leave a question open: quality for whom, judged by whom? The Guide says State leaders are accountable to all Minnesotans. In human services that includes people who receive services and their families, providers, county and lead agency partners, colleagues, and members of the public who may never contact the agency but depend on it.

A useful purpose names who it is for and what should be different for them. Start by listing the groups your work touches. Then ask whose experience you hear about most and whose you rarely hear at all. A licensing lead may hear often from providers and seldom from people living in licensed settings. A policy lead may hear from counties and seldom from the family members who complete the paperwork. Write one sentence that names a group you serve and the change you want them to notice, then a second about the colleagues you lead or work beside.

This exercise offers a personal guide for reflection; it does not change your position description, performance expectations or the agency's mission. Follow applicable law, policy, agreements and authorized direction. Decide what to share with a learning group, and check the requirements of any formal development activity before assuming your statement will remain private. The department's Equity Policy commits it to operating as a multicultural and intercultural organization, and requires equity analysis and learning. Naming who you serve can support that work, but this exercise does not replace those requirements.
lessons.keyPoint: A leadership purpose says why you lead and for whom. Naming the people served, the colleagues beside you and the public turns a general aim into something you can test against real decisions.
lessons.example: Practice case: Priya leads a small review team in disability services licensing. She does not supervise anyone, but she sets the team's priorities and speaks for it in meetings. A peer learning group has asked each member to bring a one-sentence leadership purpose. Priya's draft reads: I lead so that our team delivers accurate, timely reviews and everyone feels supported. Her manager has said the unit's priority this year is shorter review times, and a teammate tells her the draft is clear and easy to remember.
lessons.question: What should Priya do with her draft before the meeting?
choices: Keep the draft as written, since accurate and timely reviews already protect the people in licensed settings and a short purpose is easier to use.
Add who the reviews are for, such as people living in licensed settings and their families, and one change she wants them to notice.
Ask her manager for the purpose the division expects of licensing, so that her sentence matches the unit's goals before she shares it.
feedback: Accurate, timely reviews do matter. Leaving the people served unspoken, though, makes it harder to notice when a fast review and a good outcome for residents pull apart.
This keeps her focus on quality and adds the people the work exists for. A named group and a visible change give her something real to test her choices against.
Knowing the division's goals is useful, but a personal purpose is hers to write. A borrowed sentence may fit the unit and still say little about why she leads.
lessons.reflection: When you picture the people your work is for, who comes to mind first? Whose experience do you seldom hear about, and how might you learn more?
lessons.action: This week, list the groups your work affects, including people who receive services, partners, colleagues and the public. Mark the group you hear from least, and find one existing way to learn about their experience.

check.question: What most separates a leadership purpose from a general statement about doing good work?
check.correct: It names who the leadership is for and what should be different for them.
wrong: It lists the main duties and outputs of the role in order of priority.
It repeats the agency's mission wording so that it matches official goals.
check.feedback: A purpose becomes useful when it names the people it serves and the change they should notice. Duties belong in a position description and the mission is shared by everyone; your purpose says why you lead and for whom.

lessons.title: Your default picture of a good leader
objectives: Describe your own default picture of a good leader and trace where you learned it.
Identify which leadership styles your picture rewards and which it tends to overlook.
Compare course illustrations of Minimization, Acceptance and Adaptation without using them to assess people.
Adapt one routine so that more than one way of leading can be seen and credited.
lessons.teaching:
People can develop expectations about what a good leader looks like. These may form early, from family, school, faith communities, first jobs and the bosses we admired or avoided. In many workplaces the picture is confident, quick to speak, decisive and visible. Those qualities can help in some situations, but their value depends on the work and context. Cultural and organizational expectations can shape which qualities receive attention. Other traditions, and many people within any one tradition, value leaders who consult widely, speak last, build agreement or lead through steady service rather than presence.

A default picture shapes decisions without being noticed. It shows up in who we describe as having potential, whose ideas we treat as strong and who gets asked to present. Shore and Chung's 2021 review of inclusive leadership describes an assimilation pattern, in which a leader treats everyone the same and people belong only if they fit the established way. The authors note that the evidence is still at an early stage, but the pattern is easy to recognize: one style becomes the measure, and people who lead differently are read as less ready.

The intercultural development continuum, published by IDI, LLC, describes orientations toward cultural difference. The following course illustrations connect those ideas to leadership practices; they do not assess anyone. A Minimization habit sounds like: good leadership is the same everywhere, so I look for confidence and initiative. Minnesota Management and Budget's Guide lists a similar in-progress behavior, recognizing cultural differences but overemphasizing commonalities. An Acceptance habit notices that speaking first and speaking last can both be leadership. An Adaptation habit changes the routine: asking for written input before a meeting, crediting whoever built agreement, and naming results and relationships when you recognize leadership.

Examining your own picture is ordinary leadership work, not a confession. Ask whose interests your idea of a good leader serves, which colleagues it helps you see and whom it might cause you to miss. Then test it against the work: which ways of leading actually produce good outcomes for the people your team serves? For hiring, selection or acting assignments, use applicable criteria and authorized processes, consulting Human Resources when required. Managers retain their assigned responsibilities. Examine whether personal preferences are replacing relevant evidence rather than assuming that awareness alone removes bias.
lessons.keyPoint: Your picture of a good leader is learned, and it rewards some styles over others. Seeing where it came from lets you notice and credit leadership that looks different from your own.
lessons.example: Practice case: Grace is a policy lead in a human services program area. She is preparing a short team discussion on good leadership and has drafted a list: decisive, confident in meetings, quick with answers, visible to senior leaders. She shares it with Dale, a colleague who leads a county partner workgroup through patient consultation and careful follow-up. Dale says, kindly, that the list does not describe how he leads, or how many of his county partners would describe a good leader.
lessons.question: What should Grace do with her list?
choices: Keep the list as drafted, since it reflects what senior leaders in the agency tend to notice and reward in practice.
Add consultative and patient to the list, so that Dale's way of leading is included alongside the original traits.
Ask the team where each trait came from and what leadership has worked for the people they serve, then revise it.
feedback: Knowing what gets noticed is practical. Teaching it as the definition, though, keeps one style as the measure and can quietly tell quieter leaders that they are less ready.
Adding traits is a generous step. Without asking where the list came from, the default stays in charge, and new words can become a checklist rather than a change in what people see.
This treats the list as a starting point to examine. Tracing where traits came from and testing them against results for people served builds a picture the whole team can use.
lessons.reflection: Think of a leader you admired early in your working life. Which of their traits became your picture of good leadership, and what might that picture lead you to overlook?
lessons.action: Before the next meeting you lead, offer another way to contribute, such as written input in advance. Notice which ideas you hear that you usually do not. If you do not lead meetings, suggest this to whoever does, or try it with a peer.

check.question: Which course illustration best shows adapting a routine to recognize different contributions, without assessing anyone's intercultural orientation?
check.correct: Changing meeting routines and recognition so that building agreement and follow-up are credited.
wrong: Treating everyone identically and looking for the same confidence and initiative in each person.
Agreeing that leadership styles differ while keeping the same routines for meetings and recognition.
check.feedback: Changing a routine can make different contributions more visible. In these simplified illustrations, identical treatment overlooks relevant differences and recognition without action leaves the routine unchanged. One meeting practice cannot establish an individual or group orientation on the continuum.

lessons.title: Values under pressure and observable commitments
objectives: Turn two or three stated values into commitments that someone else could observe.
Identify the work pressures, such as deadlines and fatigue, most likely to pull against those commitments.
Plan a small adaptation that keeps a commitment when time is short, and a way to check that it worked.
Distinguish a values tension you can resolve yourself from one that belongs with the responsible program area or legal counsel.
lessons.teaching:
Values guide leadership only when they show up in what you do. Values such as fairness, respect and transparency need practical meaning in a particular situation. Minnesota Management and Budget's leader guide includes alignment between stated values and purpose among proficient behaviors for developing people. A commitment describes how you intend to put a value into practice.

An observable commitment turns a value into a habit someone else could see. Fairness might become: I explain how I divide work and invite questions about it. Respect might become: when a decision affects people who receive services, I use appropriate, accessible ways to seek their input while the relevant choices remain open. Transparency might become: I tell people what I do not yet know. Write each one so that a colleague watching a week of your work could tell whether you kept it. Keep it to two or three. More is hard to remember on a busy day, and a short list is easier to share with someone who can tell you when you slip.

Pressure is where commitments are tested. Deloitte's 2016 report on the six signature traits of inclusive leadership notes that time pressure and fatigue raise the risk that bias shapes a decision. Values come under the same strain: under a deadline, the quickest route usually runs through familiar people and habits. Learn your warning signs, such as skipping a step because it is only this once. Plan a feasible adaptation, such as an accessible summary and a focused question, then check who could respond and what was missed. A few responses cannot represent everyone or replace required consultation, notice, access arrangements or equity analysis.

Some tensions are yours to resolve and some are not. When a deadline limits your own practice, consider changes within your authority and explain their limits. Seek an authorized change when required participation cannot be completed. If you believe a directive conflicts with a legal requirement, raise it with the responsible program area or legal counsel rather than deciding alone. Use applicable reporting routes for discrimination concerns and consult Human Resources or labor relations about agreement requirements. Follow required reporting duties and urgent safety procedures; a conversation about personal values is not a prerequisite to reporting. A commitment gives you no authority you do not already have; it tells you when to speak up.
lessons.keyPoint: A value guides leadership only when it becomes a commitment others can see. Know which pressures pull against yours, and plan the small adaptation that keeps it when time is short.
lessons.example: Practice case: Malik manages a waiver policy team in disability services. One of his commitments is to hear from people who receive services before a change that affects them is final. His director needs revised guidance on service planning meetings by Friday. The self-advocate advisory group his team works with does not meet until next month. Malik's draft is ready, and his team is tired after a long legislative session. For this exercise, the proposed outreach is authorized, the deadline is flexible enough to consider responses, and no mandatory consultation or notice requirement is displaced. Malik must check these conditions before using a shortened process in practice.
lessons.question: What should Malik do before Friday?
choices: Send a few advisory group members a short, plain summary in formats they use, with one focused question, and tell his director the draft may change.
Submit the guidance on time and bring it to the advisory group at next month's meeting, so that members can suggest changes for the next revision.
Ask his director to move the deadline until after the advisory group meets, so that the commitment can be kept in full rather than in part.
feedback: Under the conditions in this case, this starts timely input while keeping revision possible. It does not establish that a few members represent the whole group. A focused question in an accessible format respects members' time and still brings their experience in.
Asking later is better than not asking. Once guidance is out, though, changes are harder to make, and members may hear that their input arrives after decisions are made.
Raising the deadline is fair, and the director decides. Asking only for delay, without a smaller way to hear from people now, may leave the commitment unmet if the answer is no.
lessons.reflection: Which of your values is hardest to keep when you are tired or rushed? What is the first sign that you are about to let it slip?
lessons.action: Write two or three of your values as commitments someone else could observe. For each one, note a pressure that pulls against it and the smallest step that would keep it on a hard day.

check.question: What turns a stated value into an observable commitment?
check.correct: Describing a specific action others could notice, such as explaining how work is divided.
wrong: Explaining to your team why the value matters to you and how it connects to the work.
Writing the value into a team statement posted where everyone on the team can read it.
check.feedback: A commitment is a behavior someone else could see, which makes it possible to notice when pressure pulls you off course. Explaining a value and posting a statement can help, but neither shows what you will do.

lessons.title: Writing, testing and revisiting your purpose
objectives: Write a purpose statement of two or three sentences that names who your leadership is for and one commitment.
Ask a trusted colleague what they see in how you lead, and listen without defending.
Review a recent decision against your statement and note what you would keep, change or stop.
Revise your statement or commitments based on what the decision showed you.
lessons.teaching:
A short purpose statement is easier to use than a long one. Two or three sentences are enough: one about who your leadership is for and what should change for them, one about the colleagues you lead or work beside, and one commitment that shows the purpose in action. One example: I lead so that people who use our services get answers they can act on, and so that colleagues newer to the work get real chances to grow. Write it in your own words, as you would say it to a colleague. If it would sound strange out loud, it will be hard to recall when a decision comes.

Other people can see what you cannot. Minnesota Management and Budget's Guide describes a proficient leader as one who seeks feedback, listens and modifies their approach, and its expert level includes admitting they are not always right. Shore and Chung suggest that one first step toward inclusive leadership is for leaders to ask for feedback on their own inclusiveness. Choose one person you trust who sees you work. Someone whose background or role differs from yours may notice defaults you have never had reason to question. Ask whether they are willing to offer feedback, without expecting them to represent a whole group. If they agree, share your statement and ask: where do you see this in how I lead, and where do you not? Listen and thank them before responding. Clarify what you need to understand, consider the feedback and explain any action or relevant constraint without dismissing their experience.

A purpose is tested by a real decision. After a decision that mattered, such as how work was divided, which partners were consulted or how a change was explained, reread your statement. Ask what happened, for whom, and whether the people your purpose names would recognize it in what you did. Then sort what you learned into what you will keep, what you will change and what you will stop. A gap between the statement and the decision is information, not failure.

Use this statement for personal reflection unless you knowingly include it in an agreed development or performance process. Do not assume that workplace records or shared statements are confidential. Keep unnecessary identifying details out of exercise notes while preserving authorized records and following retention, reporting and data-handling duties. If reviewing a decision raises a question about pay, classification, discipline or work assignments under a labor agreement, take it to Human Resources or labor relations instead of working it out alone. Improve ordinary work allocation within your authority and applicable requirements. Return to your statement every few months, or after any decision that tested it.
lessons.keyPoint: A purpose statement earns its place when you test it. Ask someone you trust what they see, reread it after a real decision, and keep, change or stop something based on what you learn.
lessons.example: Practice case: Ayesha supervises a team that answers eligibility policy questions from county workers. Her purpose says she leads so that families get clear, fair answers and her team can do its best work. Last week she cleared a backlog by giving the hardest cases to her two fastest staff. On a captioned video call, Lars, a peer supervisor she trusts, says the team heard about the change secondhand and two newer staff felt passed over.
lessons.question: What should Ayesha do with her purpose statement now?
choices: Rewrite the statement to focus on clear answers for families, since fairness inside the team is harder to promise during a backlog.
Keep the statement, note what the decision showed, and add a commitment to explain how urgent work is divided and why.
Set the statement aside until she has more supervising experience and a better sense of what she can realistically promise.
feedback: Narrowing the statement removes the tension instead of learning from it. The concerns about access to development would remain unexamined, and the purpose would ask less of her than she wanted.
This treats the gap as information. The statement stays honest, and a specific commitment gives the team something they can see the next time work is divided.
Waiting can feel modest, but the decision has already shown her something useful. Setting the statement aside loses the moment when it could change her practice.
lessons.reflection: Think of a recent decision that mattered. Would the people your purpose names recognize it in what you did, and what would you keep, change or stop?
lessons.action: Write a short purpose statement and invite feedback from someone willing to offer it. After a relevant decision, consider what to retain or change within your authority, keeping identifying details out of exercise notes.

check.question: After a decision falls short of your purpose statement, what is the most useful next step?
check.correct: Note what the decision showed and change one commitment so the next decision is different.
wrong: Rewrite the statement so that it matches the decisions you are able to make right now.
Keep the statement unchanged and wait to see whether the same pattern happens again.
check.feedback: A gap between your statement and a decision is information. Rewriting the purpose to fit removes what it was asking of you, and waiting lets the pattern repeat. Changing one commitment turns what you learned into practice.

cards.back: A short statement of why you lead and for whom, naming the people your work serves and what should be different for them. It guides decisions; it is not a job duty.
In Minnesota Management and Budget's leader competency model, a commitment to personal and professional growth through self-reflection and self-improvement.
The image of good leadership you learned from family, school and work. It rewards some styles, such as speaking first, and can hide others, such as building agreement.
A value written as an action someone else could notice, such as explaining how work is divided. It shows you when pressure is pulling you off course.

IDI, LLC describes orientations toward cultural difference from Denial and Polarization through Minimization to Acceptance and Adaptation. Course examples illustrate ideas; a single habit does not establish a person's or group's orientation.

aid.heading: Draft your purpose
items: List the groups your work affects: people served, partners, colleagues and the public.
Mark whose experience you hear about least and how you could learn more.
Write one sentence on who your leadership is for and what should change for them.
Add one sentence about the colleagues you lead or work beside.
Say it out loud and rewrite anything you would not say to a colleague.

aid.heading: Turn values into commitments
items: Choose the two or three values that matter most in your role.
Write each one as an action someone else could observe.
Note the pressure most likely to pull against each commitment.
Plan a feasible adaptation within your authority without replacing required consultation, access or safety steps.
Use applicable legal, discrimination and safety reporting routes; follow reporting duties without waiting to complete this exercise.

aid.heading: After a real decision
items: Reread your purpose and ask what happened, and for whom.
Ask whether the people your purpose names would recognize it in what you did.
Sort what you learned into what you will keep, change and stop.
Invite feedback from a willing colleague, listen and consider what it means for your practice.
Avoid unnecessary identifying details in exercise notes; preserve authorized records and follow data-handling and retention requirements.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget — Competency Definition Guide: Developing Leader Competencies for State of Minnesota Employees (March 2024)
sources.note: Supports the self-awareness and growth competency, leadership in any capacity, accountability to Minnesotans, alignment of values and purpose, and feedback behaviors. The official model includes development expectations; this course does not perform an employee rating.

sources.title: Deloitte University Press — Dillon and Bourke, The six signature traits of inclusive leadership (2016)
sources.note: Supports the point in lesson 3 that time pressure and fatigue raise the risk of bias in decisions. Consulting research from interviews in six countries and a small pilot; private sector, not a controlled study.

sources.title: Shore, L. M. and Chung, B. G. — Inclusive Leadership: How Leaders Sustain or Discourage Work Group Inclusion, Group and Organization Management (2021)
sources.note: Supports the assimilation pattern in lesson 2 and the advice in lesson 4 to seek feedback on your own inclusiveness. A conceptual review; the authors say the evidence is at an early stage.

sources.title: IDI, LLC — The Intercultural Development Continuum (IDC)
sources.note: Defines the five orientations and the role of individual and group assessment. The course uses simplified illustrations and does not assess anyone.

sources.title: Minnesota Department of Human Services — Equity Policy (2023)
sources.note: Supports the statement in lesson 1 that the department commits to operating as a multicultural and intercultural organization. Confirm the current version internally before citing it as current.
